newsitem.title: USA: Global chip sales seen up 4.6 percent to $138 billion.
newsitem.headline: Global chip sales seen up 4.6 percent to $138 billion.

text.p: The global chip industry is projected to grow by 4.6 percent in 1997 to $138 billion, weighed down by a flat first quarter, with the yearly growth rate then spiking above 20 percent for the next three years, the Semiconductor Industry Association said Monday.

A weakening of the Japanese yen and European currencies against the dollar caused the World Semiconductor Trade Statistics group to nearly halve its growth forecast for this year from 9 percent in real terms, the SIA said.
Had the value of the dollar remained constant -- the forecast would have been an increase from the projection last fall of a 7.4 percent rise in the U.S. market.

The midyear forcast is consistent with the industry's average annual growth rate of 17 percent since 1959, the industry group said, with total chip sales worldwide forecast to hit $245.7 billion in the year 2000.

"In the longer term, we see robust growth for the chip industry because the world's appetite for electronic devices -- from simple household appliances to digital cellular telephones and high-end computers -- shows no sign of abating," Douglas Andrey, information systems and finance director for the semiconductor association, said in a statement accompanying the release.
"Because of its amazing growth and sheer size, the chip industry has become a pivotal driver of the world economy," Andrey said.

The semiconductor industry has grown phenomenally since 1990, when it grew just 1.6 percent as global sales notched up a new annual record of $50.5 billion. By 1995, the growth rate had hit 41.7 percent and sales jumped to $144.4 billion.

But world chip sales fell to $129.2 billion in 1996 as a flurry of new plant capacity created an oversupply of memory chips, according to the World Semiconductor Trade Statistics group, a group of 70 chip makers, in its midyear forecast released through the Semiconductor Industry Association.

Microprocessors are expected to lead a rebound in worldwide chip demand, jumping 32.9 percent to $24.6 billion this year, despite the continued decline in revenues projected for dynamic random access memory (DRAM) chips.
In fact, microprocessor revenues in 1997 will for the first time exceed DRAM chip sales, the Semiconductor Industry Association said.
DRAM memory chip revenues, which tumbled 38.5 percent in 1996 to $25.1 billion, are expected to fall a further 20 percent in 1997 to $20.1 billion, according to the forecast.

But the midyear forecast also predicts that DRAM revenues will rebound in 1998 to $27.1 billion, up 35 percent from a 1997 trough, and rise by 40.4 percent in 1999 and by 32.8 percent in the year 2000, when they should hit $50.6 billion.

Geographically, the Asia Pacific market, excluding Japan, is projected to remain the world's fastest-growing sector, surpassing Europe as the third largest market this year and eclipsing Japan as the second largest in 1999.

Consumption in the year 2000 in the Americas is due to remain relatively stable at about one third of the world's chips, while sales in Japan are projected to decline to 21.5 percent from 23.9 percent this year and Europe to remain around 21 percent of the global semiconductor market.
Asia Pacific, however, is expected to grow to 24.3 percent from 21.9 percent currently, according to the forecast.
